title: How a Plumbing Trap Can Lose Water: Traps, Vents, and Common Causes

locations.name: North Carolina, USA
locations.basis: explicit mention in transcript: 'Frank in North Carolina'; video shot by This Old House may not be in North Carolina

summary: This Old House explains how a washing machine drain can pull water out of a toilet trap when a vent is absent or clogged, by using a mock-up to illustrate traps and water seals. The video defines key plumbing elements—P-traps, toilet traps, and vent pipes—and demonstrates how a vent allows air into the drainage system to prevent negative pressure and gurgling. It contrasts unvented versus vented drain conditions, discusses where vents should connect, and covers several mechanisms that can cause trap seals to fail, including oscillation from wind, siphonage with S-traps, capillary action, evaporation, and momentum. The host offers practical notes on checking vents, considering mechanical vent options, and refilling traps if sewer gas smells occur.
topics: Slug of water from washer discharge

sections.title: Frank's case: vent absence, potential fixes and vent options
sections.description: Discussion of Frank's scenario where a large slug of water from the washer lacks a vent, potential venting fixes, and the idea that vents don’t have to run straight to the roof if a mechanical vent is used.

sections.title: Seven mechanisms for losing trap seals
sections.description: Explanation of multiple causes that can progressively reduce trap seals, including wind-induced oscillation, illegal S-traps, capillary action, evaporation, and momentum, with notes on how these issues can be hidden inside traps.

sections.title: Takeaway: check, refill, and consider venting solutions
concepts: Refill traps if sewer gas smells
sections.description: Final guidance emphasizing verification of trap water, vent functionality, and practical remedies if odors or drainage issues appear.
